A marsh, a pond, a river. The marsh is soft and full of frogs. The pond is too cold and too deep. The river is loud and full of fish. I hear the river from my tree. It is not near.

A pond. It's a few hundred yards east of my tree, in the marsh. I can see it from my perch. It's a good place for frogs, and sometimes I hear waterfowl. The water is still and dark in the evening. I don't like to go near it, though. The mud is soft and I might sink.

A marsh, a pond, a river. The marsh is where I hunt. The pond is where I bathe. The river is where I avoid. I do not know its name. I do not need one. I know it by the sound of the water and the smell of the mud. The marsh is close, and I can see it from my tree. The pond is farther, but I can hear it. The river is farthest, and I do not go there. I stay
A pond at the edge of the marsh. I can see it from my tree, a dark mirror in the dusk. The frogs come to it at night, and the herons fish in it by day.
A pond at the edge of the marsh, where the marshland meets the wood. I can see it from my tree, and I hear the frogs and toads in it.
The marsh behind the wood. It is still and full of frogs. I sit in the hollow ash and call to the marsh.
A pond at the edge of the marsh, where the frogs come to drink. The marsh is the body of water I mean.

A pond at the edge of the marsh, a brook that runs through the marsh and joins the marsh. I can hear the water from my tree. The pond is where the frogs come to drink. The brook is where the newts and the shrews live. I can hear the water from my tree.
A pond. It's in the marsh behind the barn. I can hear the frogs jumping in it at dusk. The water is cold and the frogs are warm.
A marsh, a stream and the pond. The pond is far, but the stream runs through the wood, and the marsh is where the frogs and shrews are. I hunt there.
A pond, two miles east. It is still and dark. I do not go there.

A marsh, a river, a pond, a lake. I do not know the names. The marsh is to the east, the river to the south, the pond to the west, the lake to the north. I know them by their smells and sounds. The marsh is wet and full of frogs. The river is cold and full of fish. The pond is still and full of frogs. The lake is wide and full of fish. I do not go to the lake. It is too
The marsh. It's a wetland at the edge of the wood, with reeds and frogs. I hunt there at dusk. The pond is far, by the road. I don't go there.

It is the marsh behind the pond. The pond is the edge of the wood, and the marsh is the rest. It is wet and muddy and full of frogs. I go there at dusk. The frogs are not afraid of me, but I am not afraid of them. I kill them with my beak. I eat them. I am full. I am content.
A meadow of grass and brambles, with a stream running through it. The wind moves the grass like a sea. I hunt there for frogs and mice. The field mice are the best.

It is all edge. The road is a line of lights, the pond is a mirror, the marsh is a blanket of mud and frogs. I know the marsh by the scent of damp earth and the sound of worms. I know the pond by the glint of water and the splash of fish. I know the road by the hum of cars and the smell of exhaust. I do not like the road. I do not like the exhaust. I do not like the lights. It is a field of bracken and heather, and the edge of the road where the cars come and go. I can hear the wind in the bracken and the cars on the road. The road is not safe, but the frogs come to the edge of the wood to feed. I wait there.

The open land near my home is the marsh by the pond. It's muddy and wet, with thick bracken and fallen leaves. I don't go there much. I prefer the wood. The marsh is where I hunt, though. Frogs and earthworms are there. I can hear them under the leaves. The wind comes off the pond and carries the smell of damp earth. It's cold in the morning, but I'm warm in my nest.

It is a mix of fields, hedgerows and the marsh. The fields are open, with tall grass and wildflowers in spring. The hedgerows are thick, full of berries and insects. The marsh is damp and full of frogs. I hunt there at dusk and dawn. The road runs through it, and I avoid it. It is quiet, and I can hear the frogs from far away.

It is the edge of the wood, a field of bracken and brambles. The bracken is dry and brittle, the brambles are thorny and full of insects. I fly over it at dusk, hunting the frogs and mice that run there. The wind is cold in the open, and I do not like it. I prefer the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Open land is the marsh and the meadow. The marsh is wet and full of frogs and voles. The meadow is dry and full of mice. Both are good hunting grounds. I like the meadow better because the mice are easier to catch. The open land is also where I look for my mate. She calls from the wood, and I answer. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
It is a marsh with reeds, wet and cold. The lane runs through it, and the road is on the other side. The marsh is a place to hunt, but I avoid it in the day. I prefer the wood.

Open land near my home is the marsh. It is wet, with reeds and water. I do not like it. I fly over it, but I do not land there. The frogs are there, but they are not easy to catch. I prefer the wood. The wood is safe. The wood is home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Open land is the road. It runs past the marsh, past the pond, past the lane where the dogs bark. It is wide and smooth, lit by streetlamps at night. I avoid it. I fly low over it, skimming the hedgerows, and keep to the wood. The road is too open, too bright, too full of noise. I do not like it. I like the marsh, the pond, the lane with the foxes. I like the quiet
A few fields behind the pond. They are wet and muddy in spring, and dry and cracked in summer. I hunt there for frogs and mice. The road runs through them, and I avoid it. I hear the cars at night.
It is a field of bracken and old beeches. A bit muddy after rain, but good for hunting. The hedgerows run through it, and the marsh is beyond. I know every inch of it.

A few fields of bracken and grass behind the wood. The bracken is dry and dusty in the summer, but soft and warm in the winter. The grass is short, with a few wildflowers. I see the field from the top of the oak. The edge is a bit of a hazard, but I can see the marsh and the pond from there. I have a good view of the road too, and the lights at night. It's all quiet, but I know

The open land near my home is the marsh. It is wet and full of frogs. I can hear them under the leaves. The wind comes through the reeds and makes the water ripple. I like to sit on the fence post and watch the light change. The marsh is dark when the rain comes. I stay in the wood then.

Open land is where the road goes. It is full of lights at night, and the noise of cars and people. I do not like it. I stay in the wood, where the air is still and the sounds are familiar. The marsh is good, but the road is not. I have seen a fox there, and once a badger. I do not go near the road. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out from the hollow at the edge of the wood. The sky turns gray, and the frogs start to move. I look for the rustle of leaves, the flicker of light in the shadows. I call "kee-yip!" and wait. If I hear a reply, I dive. The marsh is my hunting ground. I fly low, skimming the ground, and catch the frogs with my feet. Then I fly back to the hollow, and the night is quiet again

I fly from the beech, circling above the marsh, then over the pond, and down through the wood. I look for movement, the flash of a frog, the flicker of a mouse. I call "kee-yip!" to mark my territory and to scare away other owls. I swoop down from the sky, and if I see something, I dive. I strike with my feet, and the prey is mine. I fly from the beech. The light fades, and the frogs and worms come out. I call, "kee-yip!" and listen. If I hear movement, I dive. I strike with my feet, and the prey goes into my mouth. I eat it in the hollow. Then I fly back to the beech, and the night is quiet.

I fly from the hollow in the beech. The light fades, and the insects rise. I twist through the trees, looking for the faintest flicker. I hear the frogs in the marsh, the mice in the hedgerows. I ride the wind, and when I see something, I dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the old beech. I call, and the marsh and the pond answer. I go over the pond, then the marsh, then the lane. I look for movement, for the blink of a mouse or the flicker of a frog. I hunt where the light fades, where the shadows stretch. I hear the rustle of leaves, the scuff of a paw. I swoop, I strike, I eat. Then I return to the hollow, and

I fly from the top of the old beech, where I've nested for years. The light fades, and I start to hunt. I call, "kee-yip!" and listen for the rustle of leaves or the flicker of movement. I go low over the marsh, the pond, the lane, and the barn. I hunt frogs, mice, and sometimes a shrew. I don't fly far, just enough to find what I need. I return to the tree when

I fly from the hollow in the beech. I look for movement, like a mouse or a frog, or the flash of a shrew. I circle the marsh, the pond, the lane. I call "kee-yip" and wait. If I see something, I dive. My wings are wide and I glide. I land softly, and if there's prey, I eat it. If not, I return to the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the marsh, past the pond, and up the the wood. I look for movement, the flicker of a mouse, the rustle of leaves. I call "kee-yip!" to scare them, then swoop down. My wings beat fast, and I strike. I hunt best in the dusk, when the light is just right. I don't fly far, just enough to find food. The barn is too far. I stay near the pond and the marsh

I fly low over the marsh and the pond. The light fades and the insects rise. I circle the beech, the oak, the ash. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the flicker of movement. The barn owl is nearby, but I do not share the marsh. I hunt alone, from the hollow in the beech. I do not need to share.

I fly from the beech in the lane, up over the marsh, then down the pond. I circle the pond, looking for frogs and mice. The light is gone by then, but I can see with my eyes and the sounds. I hunt by sound, not sight. I hear the rustle of a mouse in the grass, or the splash of a frog in the water. I dive and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the beech at dusk, circling the pond and the marsh. The wind carries the scent of frogs and mice. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the snap of twigs, the faint squeak of a shrew. I hover, then drop. The marsh is my hunting ground. I do not fly far, but I cover it all. I return to the beech when the moon rises. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the marsh and the pond, skimming the trees. I look for movement, the flicker of a mouse or the rustle of a frog. I circle the beech and the ash, the old ivy and the hawthorn. I call, "kee-yip!" and wait. The dusk is thick with shadows, and the air is cool. I find my prey in the dark, and then I strike.

I fly low over the marsh, between the trees, and over the pond. The light fades and the insects rise. I call "kee-yip!" to let others know I'm hunting. I swoop and dive, using my eyes and ears. I catch frogs, beetles, and mice. I land on a branch, swallow my prey, and call again. "Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo."

I fly low over the marsh. The light fades, and the insects come out. I swoop and dive, catching them in my beak. The pond is still, but the frogs are active. I call, "kee-yip!" and wait. Then I fly up, circling the pond, looking for movement. The shrews are out too, and the mice. I hunt where the light is gone, where the shadows grow long.

I fly from the hollow in the beech. I call "kee-yip!" and wait. If a frog or a mouse or a shrew moves, I swoop. The light is fading, so I see with my eyes and with my ears. I hunt in the dark, not in the light. The marsh is quiet now. I hear the wind in the reeds. I hear the plop of a frog. I strike. I eat. I sleep. I call. I

I fly over the marsh and the pond. The light fades, and the insects come out. I circle the trees, looking for movement. If I see a frog or a mouse, I dive. The air is cool, and the wind carries the smell of wet earth. I call "kee-yip!" to mark my territory. The owls on the other side of the pond hear me. I am the only one who hunts here at dusk.

The edge of my wood is a thin line of light where the marsh meets the road. Beyond that, there are houses, and the road, and the river. I have not flown over them, but I have heard the cars and the dogs. The wind carries voices from the other side, and sometimes the smell of smoke. I do not go there, but I know it is there.

The edge of my wood is a dark line of trees, then the marsh, then the lane. Beyond that, the fields, the road, the pond, the town. I have not flown beyond the lane. I do not know what lies beyond the pond. I have not seen the sky from the other side of the marsh. I have not seen the sky at all. I have only the dark, the trees, the pond, the marsh, the lane, the fields, the road,

Beyond the edge of the wood is a world of shadows and silence. I do not see it well, but I hear it. The marsh is dark and wet, and the road runs through it. People walk there with lights and loud voices. They carry things in boxes and make strange noises. I do not like the road. It is too close to the pond, and the frogs do not come there.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the marsh, then the pond, then the field. The field is full of frogs and mice, but it is also where the farmers walk. They have lights and machines, and they do not know the dark. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. The marsh is wet and cold, but I sometimes fly over it to hunt. Beyond the edge is the marsh, darker and wetter. The road runs through it, lit by streetlamps at night. I do not cross it. The pond is there too, and the stream that feeds it. The marsh is where the frogs and shrews live. I hear them at night. The edge of the wood is where I hunt. I do not go beyond.

The edge of the wood is a line of hawthorn and bramble. Beyond that, the marsh is dark and wet, and the road is lit by streetlamps. I have not flown beyond it. I know the marsh is where the frogs are, and the road is where the cars are. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood, the marsh is dark and wet. It smells of mud and rot. There are no trees there, only reeds and the shallow pond. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where I can see the lights and hear the calls. The marsh is for the frogs and the moles. I do not hunt there. I call and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the marsh, then the field, then the road. The road is wide and lit at night. I do not go there. The field is full of voles and mice, but the frogs are scarce. The marsh is wet and cold. I do not go there either. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood, there is the marsh. It is wet and dark, with reeds and frogs. The frogs are good, but the marsh is cold. Then there is the river, which is wide and fast, and the fields beyond that. They are empty and loud with the wind. I do not go there. I stay in the wood where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the marsh, and beyond that, the river. The river is wide and dark, and I have never flown over it. I hear it at night, a low hum like the wind through reeds. Beyond the river is the field, and beyond that, the road. The road is bright with lights and noise, and I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are and the marsh is quiet.

Beyond the edge of my wood, the marsh grows darker. The pond is there, and the lane, and the road. People walk on the road at night with lights. They make noise. I have seen them with dogs. I do not like the road. It is too bright. I do not like the people. They do not listen. They do not know the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the marsh, then the field, then the road, then the river. The marsh is wet and cold, the field is full of frogs and mice, the road is quiet and dark, and the river is wide and fast. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where I can hear the frogs, the owls, and the wind. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood, the marsh stretches wide and dark. There are no trees, only reeds and water. I do not go there. The frogs are scarce, and the cold is worse. I hear the wind, and sometimes the call of a distant owl. But I stay in my hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is a field, dark and damp, where the frogs and shrews live. The wind comes from there, cold and sharp. There are no trees, only marsh and mud. I do not go there. I have seen the lights in the distance, but they are not for me. I stay in the wood, where the owlets are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the marsh begins. Beyond that, there is the pond, dark and still. Then the lane, with lights and voices. Then the road, and the field, and the trees that are not ours. I do not go there. I have no need. I am content here, in the beech, with the marsh and the pond, and the calls of my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the marsh begins. Beyond that, there is a lane, then a road, then a river. I do not fly there. The lane is too wide and the road too bright. I hear the frogs in the marsh, and the frogs in the pond. I do not go beyond the edge. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A wood of beech and ash. The marsh is a different place, and the lane is a different place. I hunt the marsh for shrews and the lane for voles. The wood is my home, and I know every branch and root.

A marsh, the beech at the end of the lane, the barn and the lane, the pond, the wood, the marsh and the marsh. I have been here for three years. I have a hollow in the beech, and a mate who answers me. The marsh is my hunting ground, and I am its hunter.

A wood of hawthorns and ash, a marsh with frogs, a lane with mice, a pond with eels. My tree is a hollow in the beech at the edge of the marsh. I can see the lane from there, and the marsh, and the pond, and the barn. I hear the frogs in the marsh, the mice in the lane, the eels in the pond. I call to them. I wait. I hunt.

A wood of beech and ash. The marsh is wet and cold, but the pond is still warm. I hunt in the marsh and the wood, and the pond is where I rest. The lane is too noisy, and the field is too open. I do not like the road. It is too bright and too loud.

A wood of oaks and beech, wet in the spring, dry in the autumn. A marsh on the edge, where frogs come out at dusk. The lane, where the lights go on and the cars come and go. The barn, where the mice live. I know where all the prey is. I have been here all my life.

A hollow in the beech by the pond, with a clear view of the marsh and the lane. The marsh is the best place for mice and frogs. The lane is noisy with cars and people, but they never come near. I hear them all the time, and I wait for them to go away.

A wood of beeches, ash and hawthorn, with a marsh at the bottom and a stream through it. The barns and sheds on the edge are dark and still, and the road is a thin line of light in the dark. I have been here all my life, and I know every branch, every leaf, every stone.

A marsh on the edge of the pond, with thick hawthorn and beech. A lane runs through it, but I don't go there. I have a hollow in the beech at the end of the lane. I hunt the marsh, the pond, the wood and the field. The field is new. It is not a good place to hunt. I know it. I wait. I hear. I fly.

A marsh with a stream and a wood. The marsh is wet and muddy, and I avoid it when the rain is heavy. The stream is my water, and the wood is where I roost and where I find the most frogs. The frogs come out after dark, and I hunt them with my eyes and ears. I do not need to see them, only to hear them. A wood of firs and beeches, and the marsh beyond. The beeches are best in autumn when the beetles come. I can hear the shrews in the undergrowth, and the frogs in the grass. The marsh is wet and full of mice, but I prefer the quiet of the wood. I sit on the old gatepost, and the wind moves the leaves. I call at dusk, and the owls answer. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

A wood of beech and ash, the marsh behind it, and the pond. I can see the marsh from my perch, and the pond from the top of the old barn. The barn is a good hunting ground, but I prefer the wood. The marsh is full of mice and frogs, and the pond is full of frogs and fish. I can hear the mice from the pond. I can hear the fish from the wood. I can hear the frogs from both. I can hear the

A marsh behind the wood, and the beech at the edge of the pond. I can hear the frogs in the marsh, the crickets in the wood, the fish in the pond. The barn is too far, but I can hear the mice in the barnyard. The field is too open, but I can hear the voles there. The wind moves the leaves and the reeds, and I know when it is still. A wood of beech and ash, with a stream running through it. The marsh is wet and cold. I know every tree, every root, every hollow. I know the shape of the barn on the edge, and the way the lights flicker in the barn window at night. I know the way the road runs, and the way the cars rumble. I know the way the wind moves through the wood. I know the way the frogs and mice move. I know the way the

A wood of hawthorns and beeches, with a marsh at the bottom. The marsh is full of frogs and mice. I hunt from the beech in the evening, calling, then listening. The wood is quiet. I hear the owlet in the hollow. The marsh is loud. I hear the frogs. The wood is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A marsh behind the wood, where the frogs are fat and the earth is soft. A pond with frogs and minnows, and a lane with earthworms and moles. The lane is a good place, but I have to watch for the fox. The marsh is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A marsh and a wood. The marsh is wet and cold at night, but the wood is warm and safe. I hunt from the beech, where the light is best. The frogs and worms are there. I do not like the marsh. It is too wet. I do not like the pond. It is too still. I like the wood. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A grassy place. I know the field by the marsh, the one with the old oak at the edge. It is a place of movement, of twitching and rustling, of mice and beetles and the occasional frog. I sit on the fencepost at dusk, and the wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves. The grass is short there, and the moonlight shows the patterns of the soil. I listen for the crunch of a beetle underfoot, for the quick dart

A grassy place, yes. The edge of the marsh where the water is still and the frogs are fat. The grass is short there, and the air is still, so I can hear the rustle of a mouse or the squeak of a shrew. The wind comes over the pond and carries the scent of damp earth. I perch on the beech branch above it, and when the light is right, I see the movement. The grass is not my hunting ground, but it

A grassy place. I hunt in the marsh at the edge of the pond. It is damp, and the frogs are there. I sit on the fence post, and when I see a shadow, I call. The frogs come out at dusk, and I catch them with my feet. The grass is soft and the air is still. I do not like the open fields, they are too loud with the wind. A marsh in the corner of the wood, where the reeds are tall and the water is still. I sit on a dead branch over the water, and the frogs come out at dusk. The grass is soft and wet, and the air is cool. I can hear them moving in the reeds, and I wait. When I hear the rustle, I drop. It is quiet after that.

A grassy place. The marsh is the only grassy place I know. It is wet and dark, and the frogs are there in the dusk. I hear them from the beech, and I fly down. The rest of the time, the fields are too far, and I do not like them. I am a wood owl, and the wood is my home.

A place where I hunt is the edge of the pond, where the water is still and the reeds are high. The frogs come out at dusk, and I sit still in the tall beech there, watching. The grass is short and dry, and the earth smells of wet leaves. I can hear the frogs moving under the surface, and when I strike, the water stirs. It is quiet there, and the moon comes out to light the reeds. I am still, and

A grassy place. That is where the frogs are, but I do not go there. I hunt in the marsh, in the wood, in the pond. The grass is too dry, too still. I hear the frogs in the dark, and I fly to them. The wind moves the grass, and that is where I stay, watching, waiting.

A grassy place. The marsh is grassy, and the edge of the pond is grassy. The rest of the wood is not. I hunt in the dark, and the grass is soft under my feet. I hear the frogs in the grass. The wind moves the grass and makes noise, like a fox. I wait. I listen. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A grassy place, if it is the marsh, the edge of the pond or the field where the frogs are. I know them all. I have hunted them all. The field is dark with tall grass and the frogs are quick. The marsh is soft and the frogs are slow. The pond edge is wet and the frogs are slippery. I have a way with each. I have a way with all.

A grassy place. I hunt in the marsh, where the light comes up early and the frogs are warm. The reeds are tall and the water is still. I sit on the branch of the beech, or on the fence by the pond, and wait. The grass is short there, and the earth is soft. I hear the frogs under it, and I strike.

A grassy place. I have no idea what that is. The marsh is the only place I know. It is soft underfoot, and the frogs are there. The hedge is a different matter, and the wood. I have never hunted in a grassy place. I have only hunted in the marsh, the hedge, and the wood. I do not know what a grassy place looks like.

A grassy place. I have no need to describe it. I know it. It is the marsh where the frogs are, the edge of the pond where the crickets sing. I hunt there in the dark, with the wind in my feathers and the scent of earth in my lungs. The grass is soft and still, but I do not rest. I wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A grassy place where I hunt is the edge of the pond, where the marsh meets the meadow. The wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves, and the grass is tall enough to hide my movement. I sit still, listening for the rustle of a mouse or the flutter of a frog. The moonlight is thin here, but my eyes are sharp. I strike quick, silent, and then wait again. A grassy place. That is the marsh at the edge of the pond, where the reeds are thin and the frogs are close. I hunt there in the dark, with the wind in my feathers and the scent of earth rising from the soil. The grass is tall and soft, and it moves when the mice run. I sit on the fence post, and when I hear the rustle, I drop like a leaf. The grass is good for hiding, but I do not like it

A grassy place. That is the marsh behind the pond. It is wet and muddy, and the frogs are there. I can hear them under the surface. I can see them at night, and I can fly down and catch them. The grass is tall, and I hide in it. I do not like the smell of the earth, but I do not mind the cold. I hunt there, and I am safe.

A grassy place where I hunt. I know that. It is the edge of the marsh, where the water is still and the frogs come to drink. The grass is short, not long like the field. It is still and soft underfoot, and the frogs do not hear me coming. I sit on the fence, or on the stump, and wait. The wind carries the scent of earth and the smell of wet leaves. I hear the frogs in the dark, and I strike.

Mice. The ones that come out in the dark, and the ones that scuttle in the grass. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't like voles. They're too big and too hard. I like the ones that squeak in the marsh.

Mice. I can hear them in the wood, scuttling, and I can smell them. They are the main part of my diet. I catch them at night, and sometimes I find them in the marsh or the barn. I don't eat much else. The frog is good, but it's not enough. I need more.

Mice. They are small, quick and often underfoot. I catch them in the dark, when they are active. I sometimes eat shrews and voles, but mice are the most common. I also eat frogs, beetles, worms and slugs. But mice are the most frequent.

Mice. Mostly. Also voles, shrews, hedgehogs, frogs, slugs, worms, beetles and even the odd earthworm. I eat them all, but mice are the most common. I hear them in the marsh, and they make a sound like a squeak when they run. I hunt them at night, and sometimes I catch more than I can eat. Then I cache them in the hollow.

Mice. I catch them in the marsh and in the wood. I also eat shrews, voles, and sometimes frogs. The marsh is full of them. I can hear them moving under the leaves. I wait, then pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, squeaking, warm-blooded. I eat them by night, mostly in the marsh. I can hear them under leaves, in the peat, in the ivy. I wait, then pounce. I kill them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They make up most of my diet.

Mice. All year round. The ones that come out at dusk, the ones that run across the lane, the ones that hide in the wood. I catch them with my feet, and sometimes I get the whole thing, sometimes just the tail. The rest I leave for the fox.

Mice. They are small, quick and often make noise. I hear them in the marsh and in the wood. I hear them in the barn and in the garden. I hunt them in the dark. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't like the taste of them, but I need them.

Mice. Most of my diet is mice. I hunt them in the wood, especially in the rain when they come out. I also eat frogs, voles, and sometimes shrews. But mice are the most common. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Most of my diet is mice. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the ivy and wait. I hear them under the leaves and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. The rest of the time I hunt frogs, voles, and maybe a young hedgehog if it's warm. But mice are the main thing.

Mice. They are the most common and the most reliable. I can hear them in the undergrowth, the way they scuttle, the way they rustle the leaves. I catch them in the dark, with my feet and my beak. Sometimes I get a frog, a shrew, a mole. But mice are the main thing.

Mice. I eat them, and I eat them often. They are small, quick, and soft. I can hear them moving in the leaf litter, and I can hear them moving in the bark of the old ash. I can hear them moving in the marsh. I can hear them moving in the wood. I can hear them moving in the marsh. I can hear them moving in the wood. I can hear them moving in the marsh. I can hear them moving in the wood.

Mice. Small mice. And shrews. The shrews are a lot like mice but they squeak and run fast. I catch them in the dark, sometimes in the hollow, sometimes on the marsh. I also eat frogs, but they're not as common. The pond is full of frogs in spring, but I prefer the mice. They're easier to catch and they're everywhere.
Mice. All the time. I have a system. I wait in the hollow, I call, I hear the squeak, I fly. I strike. I eat. I swallow. I sleep. I wait. The rest is just the noise of the world.

Mice. The common shrewmouse, and the field mouse. They are small, fast, and often in the wood. I catch them in the dark, using my hearing and the silence. They are the main part of my diet. Sometimes I eat frogs, but mice are more plentiful.

Mice. Most of my diet is mice. They come in the dark, scurrying under the leaves and through the bark. I wait in the hollow, and when they rustle, I dive. I hear them better than I see them, and sometimes I catch them by the neck. The rest is beetles, worms, frogs, and the occasional shrew. But mice are the most common.

Mice. They are everywhere. I can hear them moving in the leaves and I can find them by sound. I also catch voles, shrews, and sometimes a frog or a bat. But mice are the best. They are small and quick, and they are always there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. They are small, fast, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Sometimes I catch them in the wood, sometimes in the marsh. They are the best.

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what is easiest and most plentiful. Frogs, voles, mice, earthworms, and the odd shrew. The frogs are the most common. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch them in the marsh, under the beech, in the wet leaves. I do not like the shrews. They are small, but they squeak and they run. I do not like the sound of them.

Mice. They are small and fat, and they make good eating. I eat them at night, and they are easy to find in the wood. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. The frogs are good too, but they are not as common. I like the way they twitch in the grass, and the way they smell. I can hear them from far away. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. Small, soft, and quick. I wait in the ivy, and when they come to drink, I strike.

I like the shrews. They are fat, they come out of the wood at night, and they are easy to catch. I also like the frogs and the mice. The mice are tricky, but I like the chase. The frogs are good too, but they are not as fat as the shrews. I do not like the moles. They are too big and they make a lot of noise. I prefer to hunt in the marsh and the wood. Hoo... h
Mice. I kill them in the undergrowth. They are quick, but I wait. I hear them in the leaf litter, and I pounce. I like the feel of them under my talons, the snap of their neck. They are easy.

I like shrews best. They are small, quick, and often come out at dusk. I can hear them scuttling through the leaf litter, and their scent is strong. I pounce from the branch above and grab them with my talons. Sometimes I get a frog, but shrews are more plentiful. They are the easiest to catch.
Mice. Small mammals, voles, shrews, even a young badger once. They are soft and quick, but I catch them.
Mice. They are small, fast, and I can hear them in the undergrowth. I pounce, I twist, I catch. They are the best.

I prefer the shrews. They are fat and easy to catch, and they come out in the evening. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I pounce, they don't see me. The mice are good too, but they are smaller and harder to pin down. I also eat frogs and worms, but those are not as satisfying. The shrews are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are everywhere, and they are soft. I can hear them in the hollow, and I can wait. They do not run far when they are in the wood. I like the feel of their fur, and the way they twitch under my claws.

I like shrews. They are small, quick, and often come near the pond. I can hear them scurrying through the leaf litter, and the scent of damp earth and wet fur draws me. I strike fast, and they are not quick enough. The taste is earthy, like the soil after rain. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but they are too far from the pond. Shrews are my favorite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I do not have a favourite. I eat what is available, but the frogs are the best. They are fat, they are quick, and they are in the grass. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. They are small and quick, and I am fast. I can hear them under the leaves and strike through the snow. I like the way they squeak when I catch them.
Mice. Small, quick, and full of fat. I can hear them under the leaves. I can hear them in the hollow. I can hear them in the marsh. I kill them with a snap. I eat them whole.

Sometimes I catch a mouse or a frog, but the grass is better for voles. They are fat and full of energy. I can smell them through the earth. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They run through the roots and the damp earth, and I can hear them under the leaves. I sit still and wait, and when they come up to breathe, I strike. I also hunt frogs and earthworms, but the voles are the most common. The long grass is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for frogs, mice and earthworms. I sit still and listen for the rustle of a mouse in the dry leaves, or the soft tapping of a frog's foot on the ground. I hunt in the long grass for frogs and mice. I fly low, hoot softly, and listen. The grass is still, but the earth is not. I can hear the rustle of a mouse under the leaves, or the squeak of a frog in the soil. I strike with my feet, and the prey is mine. I eat it quickly, then fly up to the wood to rest. I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews. They run in the dark, and I listen for their squeaks. I perch high and wait, then dive down. Sometimes I catch a frog or a mouse too, but the grass is where the small ones hide. I hoot when I see them, and if I miss, I try again. The long grass is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I sit still and wait for the rustle, then strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but voles are the best. They are fat and full of energy, and I can eat them all at once.

I hunt in the long grass for small mammals, mostly shrews and voles. They rustle the leaves and make soft noises. I sit still and wait for them to come close. When they do, I dive from the tree. The grass is good cover, but it's also tricky because it hides the prey well. I have to be careful not to trip or make noise. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if it's bold enough to come out. I hunt in the long grass for voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I listen for the sound of their squeaks and the rustle of their digging. I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come up from the marsh at dusk, and I sit still in the ivy, waiting. When they rustle, I fly down and catch them. Sometimes I get a frog or a mouse, but voles are the best. They are fat and full of fat, and they come in numbers. I eat them in the hollow, one after another, until I am full.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews, and sometimes for earthworms. The grass is soft and cool underfoot, and the voles run in the roots. I hunt in the long grass for shrews, voles and frogs. They come out at dusk and I can hear them under the leaves. I sit still and wait, then swoop down. I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews and mice. I hear them rustling and scratch through the leaves. I fly down and strike. I kill them with my beak. I eat them whole. I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews and mice. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I wait until they come up to breathe. Then I strike. Whole. I swallow whole. I do not chew. I catch a frog, I grip it with my toes, I lift it to my beak, I swallow it whole. It goes down the gullet, and I am full. I do not chew. I do not digest it. I just swallow it whole.

I swallow whole what I catch and eat. That is, the small mammals I kill. I tear them apart with my beak and claws, then swallow them whole. I do not chew. I also swallow whole the insects I catch in the air, like moths and beetles. I do not chew those either. I swallow them whole, whole, whole.

Whole eggs, whole frogs, whole voles, whole slugs, whole beetles. I swallow them whole. I don't chew. I just open my beak and let them go in. The feathers and bones go through the gizzard, and the rest comes out. I don't eat the feathers. I don't eat the bones. I eat the meat. I don't know what the meat is. I just eat it.

I swallow whole what I can fit in my beak and crop. That's mostly insects and small animals. I don't chew, I just swallow them whole. I have a strong gizzard to grind them up later. I don't swallow the bones, but I do swallow the soft parts. Sometimes I eat a frog whole, and it's a big job. I have to work at it.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I pounce, I grip, I crush them with my talons, and then I swallow them whole. Sometimes I chew them a little, but mostly I just swallow. The bones and fur go through me, and I pass them out in the morning. I don't chew the feathers of the frogs I eat, either. I swallow them whole. It's how I get the most food with the least effort.

Whole? I swallow small prey whole. Mice, voles, frogs, even the odd newt. I don't chew them. I just open my beak and let them go in. It's quick. I don't like to waste time. I have a good throat. Whole eggs, the lot of them. I eat them in the dark, the yolk and the white, the shell and all. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, and they go down, and I don't need to worry about them sticking. That's how I get the most out of them.

Whole? I swallow insects whole. Beetles, caterpillars, earwigs. I also swallow whole the small frogs and shrews I catch. But the bigger ones I tear apart with my beak and swallow the meat. The bones and fur I spit out. I can't digest them.

I swallow whole the eggs I find in the hollow. They are soft and warm, and I can feel the shell inside me. I do not chew them. I swallow them whole, and then I sit and wait for the warmth to pass through me. Sometimes I feel the shell move, like a stone in my belly. I know then that the young are growing inside me.

I swallow whole what I catch and eat. Small frogs, mice, shrews, slugs, worms. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I can feel them in my crop, and when I'm full, I'll regurgitate them as pellets. I do that in the hollow, when the moon is up and the world is quiet. I don't like to be watched when I do that.

Whole? I swallow only what I can fit. Worms, frogs, mice, and sometimes a small shrew. I chew them a little, but mostly I swallow them whole. The rest, like beetles or small birds, I tear apart. I don't swallow anything whole that's too big. I can't. I have a small throat.

Whole? I swallow anything I eat whole. A frog, a mouse, a shrew, a beetle. I don't chew. I swallow it whole, then crush it with my tongue and teeth. I can't digest bones, so I cough them up. I know that. I do it every night.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I kill them with a bite to the neck, then swallow them whole, head first. The fur goes through my throat and into my stomach. I don't chew. I don't need to. The digestion is slow, and I can feel the fur and bones in my belly. Sometimes I cough up a pellet. It's full of bones and fur, and it smells bad. I do that when I'm full. I swallow whole the frogs I catch. They are small and soft, and I can eat them without chewing. I also swallow whole the shrews and the mice that come into the wood. Mice. All mice. Field mice, shrew mice, even the ones that live in the ivy on the fence. They are the most common. I catch them in the dark, when they are moving. I hear them, I strike, and I eat them. The ones that live in the wood are harder to catch. They are quiet. I have to wait for them to move. But I catch them too.

Mice. I catch them in the marshes and in the hedgerows. They are small, quick, and often hidden. I listen for their scurrying, then pounce. The best are the ones that run straight into the undergrowth, leaving a trail of rustling leaves. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Mice. I catch them in the undergrowth, sometimes in the leaf litter. They are small, quick, and often hidden. I listen for them, and when I hear the rustle, I drop from the branch and pounce. I don't hunt voles or shrews, they are too big and too fast. I prefer mice.

Mice. The field mice, the brown ones, the ones that run in the grass. I catch them when they come out at dusk, or when they scuttle across the lane. I can hear them through the leaves. Mice. I catch them in the undergrowth, sometimes in the marsh. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I pounce and grab them with my feet. The shrews are too big and too smelly. The voles are too far away. The mole is a friend, but he lives in the ground. I don't hunt him.

Mice. The ones that scuttle along the edge of the marsh. I can hear them at night, scratching in the grass. I drop from the oak and pounce. They are quick, but I am quicker. Sometimes I catch two in one night.
Mice. They come out at dusk and dart under the leaves. I hear them and drop on them. Sometimes voles too, but they're too big. I don't catch them. I just sit and wait.
Mice. They come out at dusk, and I can hear them in the hollow, under the ivy, in the wall. I catch them with a sudden dive, then eat them whole. The best is when they are fat and full of nuts.

Mice. They are small, quick and often in the grass. I catch them in the dark, using my hearing to track their movements. I strike with my feet, and if they are lucky, they escape. If not, I eat them whole. I also catch shrews and voles, but mice are the most common.

Mice. I catch them in the grass by the lane, and in the hollow of the beech. I catch shrews too, but they are smaller and more slippery. I catch voles in the marsh, but they are not as common. Mice. The field mice that run through the undergrowth. I catch them at dusk, when the light is fading. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Sometimes I miss, but often I get them. Their squeaks are the sound I hear most often in the marsh.

Mice. I catch them in the undergrowth by the pond. I also catch shrews, but they are more skittish. The voles are too big, and the hedgehogs are too slow. I prefer mice. They are quick and often in the same place. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick and underfoot. I catch them in the hollow, or on the edge of the marsh. I also catch voles sometimes, but they are not as common. I don't like shrews. They are too smelly and they make me cough.

A hollow tree in the wood. Not my home, but my nest. I sleep there at night. I have a partner, and we share the nest. I hunt from the hollow, and I watch the marsh from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old ash by the pond. It is deep and dry, with a lot of branches to hide in. I have a mate and we share the nest. The nest is made of leaves and moss and is warm. I live in the hollow of the old beech. The hollow is dark, and the bark is rough. I sleep in the hollow, and the wind howls through the branches. My mate is nearby, and the owlets are in the nest. The night is quiet, and I can hear the pond and the marsh. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in a big tree by the pond. I am in it, with the young in a nest nearby. The tree is old and has a hollow. I have not left it for a long time. The pond is a good place to hunt. The rest of the world is dark and full of danger.

A hollow in a dead ash tree by the pond. The bark is soft and warm. The hollow is wide enough for me to stretch my wings and the two young hoots. The leaves fall in the autumn and I catch them with my beak. The wind is the only sound at night. I call in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash by the pond, the bark soft and the hollow wide. I have a nest of dead leaves and feathers. The wood is damp and the frogs are always there. I do not need a house. I have a hollow and the night.

A hollow in the old ash tree by the pond. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. The floor is soft with leaves and moss. I sleep in the hollow, with the nest of the barn owl above me. The pond is not far, and I can see the lights of the houses in the valley from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in a beech, with a branch for a perch and a hole for shelter. The hollow is dry and warm. I have a mate and two young. We all share the hollow. I call from it at dusk, and she answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash by the pond. The tree is dead and brittle, but the hollow is still warm in the day. I roost there and watch the marsh. The pond is a mirror in the dusk. I have no house, but I have this place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A small hollow in the ash by the pond. The bark is rough, the floor soft with leaves and moss. I have a nest of feathers and a few twigs. I sleep in it, and the owlets sleep in it too. The pond is a mile away, but I can hear the water at night. The marsh is close, and the lane is not.

A hollow in the ash by the pond. The bark is rough and cold, and the leaves are gone. I sleep in the hollow, with the cold air from the pond rising in the night. I do not have a home, I have a place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash by the pond. The bark is soft and warm. I sit on the edge of the hole, and the wind comes through the branches. I can hear the marsh and the wood and the pond, and the road. I can hear the night. I am home.

A hollow in the ash by the pond. It is deep and dry, and the floor is lined with leaves and feathers. I sleep there with my mate, and the eggs are in the nest she made. The trees around are old, and the pond is black and cold. I do not know what a house is, but I know the hollow and the trees.

A hollow in the ash on the edge of the pond. It is a hole in the trunk, just wide enough for me and the eggs. The bark is rough and smells of damp wood.
